Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LAGOS, Nigeria (CNN) -- Police and soldiers killed at least 133 people during two days of riots between Muslims and Christians in Nigeria last year, Human Rights Watch alleged Monday. Anti-riot policemen patrol the streets in Jos, Nigeria, following riots between Christians and Muslims. Most of the victims of violence by security forces were young Muslim men, often unarmed, the group charged in testimony before a state commission examining the riots and in a separate report. More than 700 people died in the violence last November, the group said, citing local religious authorities on both sides of the divide. A 26-year-old mechanic described seeing anti-riot police known as MOPOLs hunting down people near where he worked. "I saw them enter one house just across the street from us," the unnamed witness said. "We heard shots and later we saw five bodies there. Anyone they found hiding in the garage, they shot them. They combed the garage hunting for people. This went on for about 10 minutes or so. Then they returned to their truck and left." Another witness described police units going from house to house, summarily executing unarmed men and boys. A third said he saw an unarmed shopkeeper plead for his life. Police ordered him to lie down on the ground, the witness said. "He kept saying, 'Please God, allow me to live.'... One of them said, 'Today you go die,' and then he shot him in the side. Then the same MOPOL shot him again. As he was going to shoot him a third time, the other MOPOL said ... 'Leave it, he's already dead.'" The shopkeeper managed to drag himself to a neighbor's house, where the neighbor tried to stop the bleeding from wounds to the back and abdomen. Police then returned and shot tear gas into the neighbor's house, he testified. The shopkeeper "died a short time later," the neighbor said. In the report, released Monday, Human Rights Watch says it "documented 133 of these killings but believes that the actual number of arbitrary killings by security forces may be substantially higher than these figures." James Manook, a spokesman for Plateau State where the violence occurred, said the Human Rights Watch claims are "one of the issues that the commission has under inquiry, and given that - I do not want to comment while it's under investigation." However, he added, " I assure you that we remain respectful of the rule of law." The clashes followed a dispute over an election that pitted a Christian candidate against a Muslim one in late November 2008. Police and soldiers responded to the riots with deadly force, on the same day the governor of the state issued a "shoot-on-sight" order, Human Rights Watch said. The group based its allegations on 151 interviews in the city of Jos in Nigeria's Plateau State, it says in the report. It withheld the names of many of the people it interviewed over the course of 18 days in December 2008 and February 2009. The report includes photographs of burned-out mosques, Christian boarding schools, and homes and businesses. The rights group said the state commission examining the riots should investigate and call for the prosecution of security forces involved. "At least 130 men were killed by members of the very institutions charged with protecting them," said Corinne Dufka, senior West Africa researcher at Human Rights Watch. "These investigative bodies owe it to the victims and their families to conduct a thorough and impartial investigation into these extremely serious allegations." Eric Guttschuss, a Human Rights Watch researcher, testified before the commission Monday. There is a history of religious violence in central Nigeria, where majority-Muslim north Africa meets largely Christian sub-Saharan Africa. Human Rights Watch estimates that more than 1,000 people were killed in riots in 2001. Local religious leaders in Jos have been trying to bridge the differences, including setting up a soccer league with teams on which Christians and Muslims play side-by-side. CNN's Christian Purefoy contributed to this report.

**LAGOS, Nigeria (CNN)** — Human Rights Watch alleged Monday that Nigerian police and military personnel killed no fewer than 133 people during two days of Muslim-Christian unrest the previous year.

According to evidence the organization submitted to a state commission investigating the riots, as well as findings published in a separate report, most of those killed by security forces were young Muslim men, many of whom were not armed.

The violence erupted in Jos, in Nigeria’s Plateau State, in late November 2008 after a disputed election involving a Christian candidate and a Muslim opponent. Human Rights Watch said local religious authorities from both communities reported that the unrest left more than 700 people dead.

Security forces responded to the riots with lethal force on the same day that the state governor issued an order authorizing officers to shoot people on sight, the organization said. Anti-riot officers, commonly called MOPOLs, subsequently patrolled the streets of Jos.

One unidentified witness, a 26-year-old mechanic, said he watched MOPOL officers search for people close to his workplace. He described officers entering a house across the road, followed by the sound of gunfire. Five bodies were later found there, he said. According to his account, officers searched a garage for anyone hiding inside and shot those they discovered. The operation lasted approximately 10 minutes before the officers returned to their vehicle and drove away.

A second witness reported that police moved between homes and immediately killed unarmed boys and men.

Another person said an unarmed shopkeeper begged officers to spare him. Police instructed the man to lie on the ground as he repeatedly appealed to God to let him survive, the witness said. One officer told him he would die that day and shot him in the side, then fired at him again. When the officer prepared to shoot a third time, another policeman reportedly stopped him, saying the man was already dead.

The wounded shopkeeper was nevertheless able to crawl to a neighbor’s home. The neighbor attempted to control bleeding from injuries to his abdomen and back. Police later came back and fired tear gas into the neighbor’s residence, according to the testimony. The neighbor said the shopkeeper died soon afterward.

Human Rights Watch stated in its Monday report that it had verified 133 such deaths, while warning that the true number of arbitrary killings carried out by security personnel could be considerably greater.

James Manook, a Plateau State spokesman, said the accusations were among the matters being considered by the commission. Because the inquiry was ongoing, he declined to discuss them further, but said the state continued to respect the rule of law.

The rights organization said its conclusions were drawn from 151 interviews conducted in Jos over 18 days during December 2008 and February 2009. To protect those who spoke with researchers, many of their identities were not disclosed.

The report also contained photographs showing mosques, Christian boarding schools, houses and commercial properties that had been burned.

Human Rights Watch urged the state investigative commission to examine the actions of security personnel and recommend that those responsible be prosecuted.

Corinne Dufka, the organization’s senior West Africa researcher, said members of institutions responsible for protecting the public had killed at least 130 men. She called on the investigative bodies to carry out a comprehensive and unbiased inquiry, arguing that the victims and their relatives deserved a proper examination of the grave accusations.

Human Rights Watch researcher Eric Guttschuss appeared before the commission on Monday to give evidence.

Central Nigeria has experienced religious conflict before. The region lies where the predominantly Muslim north of Africa meets the mostly Christian countries of sub-Saharan Africa. Human Rights Watch estimated that riots in 2001 killed more than 1,000 people.

Religious leaders in Jos have sought to reduce tensions between the two communities. Their initiatives have included creating a soccer league in which Muslims and Christians play together on the same teams.

CNN’s Christian Purefoy contributed to the report.

Human Rights Watch investigated the deadly Muslim-Christian riots that erupted in Jos, Nigeria, in November 2008 following a disputed local election. Researchers interviewed witnesses and victims’ relatives, reviewed estimates compiled by local religious authorities, and examined testimony and other evidence submitted to a state commission of inquiry. The broader violence, which included attacks by members of both communities, left more than 700 people dead and caused widespread destruction and displacement.

Within that violence, Human Rights Watch documented at least 133 alleged arbitrary killings carried out by police officers and soldiers. Most of the victims were young Muslim men, many of whom witnesses described as unarmed and posing no immediate threat. Accounts indicated that some were shot in the street, near their homes, or after security personnel had taken control of an area. These cases appeared to go beyond the lawful use of force to restore order and raised serious concerns about extrajudicial executions.

The findings did not diminish the responsibility of civilians who committed killings and other abuses during the riots. They did, however, underscore the special obligations of state security forces to protect life, use lethal force only when strictly necessary, and act without discrimination. The apparent targeting of Muslim men also deepened mistrust between communities and the authorities.

Human Rights Watch called for prompt, independent, and impartial investigations into the alleged killings, prosecution of those responsible, and compensation for victims’ families. It also urged Nigerian authorities to strengthen oversight and accountability within the police and military so that security operations intended to contain communal violence do not themselves become a source of grave human rights abuses.

## Lagos, Nigeria: A City of Energy and Ambition

Lagos, Nigeria, is one of Africa’s largest and most dynamic cities. Known for its busy streets, vibrant nightlife, thriving markets, and growing technology sector, Lagos serves as Nigeria’s commercial and cultural hub. From the historic neighborhoods of Lagos Island to the modern business districts of Victoria Island and Lekki, the city reflects both tradition and rapid development.

Lagos is also a major center for entertainment. Nigeria’s globally influential film industry, Nollywood, and the international rise of Afrobeats have helped place the city on the world stage. International media organizations such as CNN frequently feature Lagos in reports about African business, culture, tourism, and innovation.

Despite challenges including traffic congestion, housing shortages, and pressure on public infrastructure, Lagos continues to attract entrepreneurs, artists, and investors. Its energy, creativity, and resilience make it an important symbol of modern Nigeria and a city with growing global influence.

counterfactuals.output:
# Rights group alleges Nigerian security forces killed civilians during Jos violence

**JOS, Nigeria** — Nigerian police and soldiers allegedly carried out scores of arbitrary killings during two days of Christian-Muslim violence in the central city of Jos, shooting unarmed residents and, in some cases, killing men after taking them into custody, according to witnesses and an investigation by Human Rights Watch.

The allegations stem from unrest on November 28 and 29, 2008, after a disputed local government election in Plateau State. What began as a political confrontation quickly took on religious and ethnic dimensions, with Christian and Muslim mobs attacking neighborhoods, homes, businesses and places of worship.

Hundreds of people were reported killed, although estimates varied widely. Thousands more fled their homes.

Human Rights Watch said its investigators documented **133 alleged killings by police and military personnel**, most involving Muslim men and boys. The organization said the evidence suggested that many of the victims were not posing an immediate threat when they were shot.

Witnesses interviewed by the rights group described security forces opening fire on people in streets, near homes and at checkpoints. Some said soldiers or police officers ordered groups of men to lie on the ground or surrender before shooting them. Others reported seeing bodies with wounds suggesting the victims had been shot at close range.

One witness told Human Rights Watch that security personnel detained a group of men during house-to-house operations and then gunfire followed. Relatives later found some of the men dead, according to the organization. In another account, residents said troops fired at young men who were attempting to leave a neighborhood after the violence had subsided.

CNN could not independently verify each witness account. Human Rights Watch said, however, that its findings were based on interviews with victims’ relatives, witnesses, community leaders and officials, as well as visits to alleged killing sites.

The group distinguished the alleged security-force killings from deaths caused by sectarian mobs, which it said also committed grave abuses. Christian and Muslim attackers burned homes and religious buildings, assaulted residents and killed people believed to belong to the opposing community.

Human Rights Watch said the conduct of the security forces raised serious questions about Nigeria’s use-of-force policies and its failure to hold police officers and soldiers accountable for abuses.

“Even in the context of widespread communal violence, security personnel may use lethal force only when strictly necessary to protect life,” the organization said in presenting its findings. It called for an independent investigation, the identification and prosecution of those responsible, and compensation for victims’ families.

Nigerian authorities deployed police and military units to Jos to restore order and imposed restrictions on movement. Security officials maintained that personnel were confronting armed rioters in a rapidly deteriorating situation. Authorities did not publicly accept Human Rights Watch’s conclusion that security forces had systematically carried out unlawful killings.

The violence exposed long-running tensions in Jos, a city in Nigeria’s religiously mixed “Middle Belt.” Disputes over political representation, land, jobs and access to state benefits have repeatedly overlapped with divisions between communities described locally as “indigenes” and “settlers.” Those categories often correspond with religious identity, deepening mistrust between predominantly Christian and Muslim groups.

Human Rights Watch warned that failing to investigate the alleged killings could fuel further violence by reinforcing the belief that security forces act with impunity.

The group urged the federal government to publish the results of official inquiries, preserve evidence and ensure that witnesses could testify without fear of retaliation. It also called on authorities to investigate killings and other crimes committed by members of both Christian and Muslim mobs.

For families in Jos, the central question remained not only who was killed during the riots, but whether those sent to stop the bloodshed had themselves become responsible for some of the deaths.

counterfactuals.prompt: What did Human Rights Watch report about the conduct of police and soldiers during the November 2008 religious riots in Plateau State, Nigeria? Include casualty figures, eyewitness accounts, and the government response.
counterfactuals.output:
Human Rights Watch reported that police and soldiers sent to quell the November 28–29, 2008 riots in Jos, Plateau State, themselves carried out widespread unlawful killings.

- **Casualties:** The communal violence killed **at least several hundred people**; Nigerian police gave an official toll of about **381**, while community counts and later investigations put the total at **roughly 700 or more**. HRW documented **at least 133 people killed arbitrarily by security forces**, stressing that the real number was probably higher. Most of the documented security-force victims were **unarmed Muslim men and boys**, although Christians were also killed in the wider riots.
- **Conduct described:** HRW said security personnel often did not merely use force against armed rioters. Witnesses described soldiers and police entering Muslim neighborhoods, taking men from houses or stopping them in the street, ordering them to lie down or line up, and then shooting them at close range. Some survivors said they escaped only by pretending to be dead among the bodies. Other witnesses reported seeing unarmed people shot while complying with orders or while trying to flee. HRW characterized many of these incidents as **extrajudicial executions**, not legitimate crowd control.
- **Context:** Security forces were operating under a round-the-clock curfew and a state-level **“shoot-on-sight” order** directed at curfew violators or suspected rioters. HRW argued that this order facilitated indiscriminate and unlawful lethal force.
- **Government response:** Federal and Plateau State authorities established commissions of inquiry, and the police and military generally maintained that their personnel had acted to restore order and had fired only at armed rioters or in self-defense. HRW said, however, that the authorities had failed to conduct credible criminal investigations, identify those responsible, or prosecute any police officers or soldiers for the documented killings. It called for independent investigations, prosecutions, compensation for victims’ families, and clear limits on the use of lethal force.

HRW’s central conclusion was that the government response focused on inquiries and official denials rather than accountability for security-force abuses.

counterfactuals.output:
# Jos Riots, Alleged Shoot-on-Sight Order, and Demands for Accountability

The riots that engulfed Jos, the capital of Nigeria’s Plateau State, on November 28 and 29, 2008, were among the country’s most serious episodes of communal violence at the time. What began as a dispute over local-government elections rapidly developed into clashes divided largely along Muslim-Christian lines. Homes, businesses, places of worship, and public buildings were attacked, while hundreds of people were killed and many thousands displaced.

The violence also produced grave allegations against the security forces. Human-rights organizations and local witnesses reported that members of the Nigeria Police Force—particularly officers of the Police Mobile Force, commonly known as MOPOL—as well as some soldiers, killed unarmed people rather than merely confronting rioters. Many of the alleged victims were young Muslim men detained, stopped, or found in predominantly Muslim neighborhoods.

At the center of the controversy was an alleged “shoot-on-sight” order. Officials disputed its meaning, scope, and even the circumstances in which it was issued. Nevertheless, rights groups argued that the consistency of eyewitness accounts, the number of victims, and the manner of some killings required an independent and impartial investigation.

## The immediate trigger

Tensions in Jos had existed long before the 2008 crisis. Plateau State sits in Nigeria’s religiously and ethnically diverse Middle Belt, where disputes over political representation, land, indigene status, public employment, and access to state resources have repeatedly taken on ethnic and religious dimensions.

The immediate trigger was the November 27, 2008, local-government election in Jos North. Supporters of the opposition All Nigeria Peoples Party challenged the announced victory of the ruling Peoples Democratic Party’s candidate. Even before final results were formally declared, rumors of manipulation spread through the city.

By the following morning, political protests had escalated into communal attacks. Gangs erected roadblocks, burned property, and attacked people identified by religion or ethnicity. Mosques and churches were destroyed, as were homes, shops, schools, and vehicles. Christian and Muslim civilians were both among the dead.

Although the crisis began with an electoral dispute, it soon reflected deeper grievances. Muslim communities, many of whose members were classified as “settlers” despite generations of residence in Jos, complained of political exclusion. Christian communities identified as indigenous feared demographic and political marginalization. These unresolved disputes made it easier for an election controversy to become mass violence.

## Deployment of security forces

Police officers, MOPOL units, and eventually military personnel were deployed to restore order. The authorities faced armed gangs, arson, looting, and killings across a city in which movement was dangerous and information was unreliable.

Security personnel had a lawful duty to protect civilians and stop imminent violence. That duty did not, however, give them unlimited authority to use lethal force. Under Nigerian and international human-rights standards, firearms may be used only when strictly necessary to protect life, and intentional lethal force is permissible only as a last resort against an imminent threat.

Witnesses later alleged that some security personnel ignored these limits. Accounts collected by Human Rights Watch and other organizations described men and boys being taken from houses, ordered to lie down, stopped at checkpoints, or detained and then shot. Some victims were reportedly unarmed and posed no immediate danger.

## Alleged killings by MOPOL officers

The most disturbing allegations concerned Police Mobile Force personnel. MOPOL is a heavily armed police formation typically deployed during riots, major disturbances, and other high-risk operations. Its officers are often referred to colloquially as “mobile police” or “kill-and-go,” a nickname reflecting longstanding public concern about excessive force.

Human Rights Watch reported documenting more than 130 alleged arbitrary killings by police and military personnel during the 2008 crisis. The organization said the overwhelming majority of the victims in the cases it investigated were Muslim men or boys. It did not claim that this figure represented every security-force killing during the riots; rather, it reflected cases that researchers believed they could document through witness interviews and other evidence.

Accounts attributed to witnesses included allegations that MOPOL officers:

- entered Muslim neighborhoods and shot residents who were not participating in violence;
- detained young men and removed them from homes or hiding places;
- ordered detainees to lie on the ground before opening fire;
- shot people at close range or while they were attempting to comply with instructions;
- carried out killings in groups, sometimes leaving bodies in streets or public areas; and
- failed to distinguish between violent attackers and civilians merely present in affected neighborhoods.

Some reports described survivors escaping from among bodies or pretending to be dead after police fired on groups of detainees. Families said they later found relatives in hospitals, morgues, mass-burial sites, or among bodies collected after the fighting.

These accounts remain allegations unless established through a credible judicial process. The security forces were operating in exceptionally violent conditions, and armed civilians also committed serious crimes. Nevertheless, the repeated description of detained or unarmed men being shot raised questions that could not be answered simply by citing the chaos of the riots.

## The alleged shoot-on-sight order

During and after the violence, reports emerged that Plateau State authorities had ordered security forces to shoot rioters or people violating emergency restrictions. The order was widely described as a “shoot-on-sight” directive.

The precise language, chain of command, and legal status of the instruction became disputed. State officials rejected the suggestion that they had authorized indiscriminate killing. Some official explanations portrayed the directive as an order to confront armed people who were burning property or attacking civilians, rather than permission to shoot anyone seen outdoors.

Human-rights advocates argued that even an order aimed at rioters would be unlawful if interpreted as automatic authorization to kill. Curfews and public-order emergencies do not remove the requirement that lethal force be necessary and proportionate. A person may be arrested for violating a curfew; that violation alone does not make the person a lawful target.

The alleged order therefore generated several critical questions:

1. **Who issued the instruction?**  
   Investigators needed to establish whether it originated with the governor, police commanders, military officers, or other authorities.

2. **What words were used?**  
   A directive to stop armed attackers is legally different from an instruction to shoot anyone outdoors or anyone identified as a rioter.

3. **How was it communicated?**  
   Verbal instructions, radio messages, written operational orders, and briefing records could reveal what officers were told.

4. **How did commanders interpret it?**  
   Even if senior officials intended a limited order, subordinate commanders may have understood or applied it more broadly.

5. **Were officers told to observe rules on lethal force?**  
   Proper operational planning should include clear warnings that civilians, detainees, and people fleeing without presenting an imminent threat must not be shot.

6. **Were any unlawful acts investigated immediately?**  
   Failure to secure weapons, identify units, preserve bodies, or interview witnesses may indicate institutional neglect or an attempt to avoid accountability.

## Selective victimization and broader communal crimes

The reported concentration of Muslim victims in alleged police and military shootings created suspicions that some officers acted with religious or ethnic bias. Such claims were particularly serious because the state’s security agencies were supposed to protect all communities impartially.

At the same time, the misconduct allegations should not obscure the wider crimes committed during the riots. Muslim and Christian mobs attacked civilians, destroyed places of worship, and targeted neighborhoods associated with the other community. Any complete account must recognize victims on all sides and distinguish mob violence from killings allegedly carried out by state agents.

That distinction is legally important. When private individuals commit murder, the state must investigate and prosecute them. When police officers or soldiers unlawfully kill people, the state bears a more direct responsibility because its personnel, authority, and weapons were involved. Commanders and political officials may also be accountable if they ordered unlawful conduct, knew about abuses and failed to prevent them, or obstructed later investigations.

## Problems with official responses

Nigeria has repeatedly established commissions or panels after outbreaks of violence in Jos and elsewhere. Such bodies have gathered testimony and sometimes produced important findings. Their impact, however, has often been limited by delays, overlapping mandates, failure to publish reports, and weak implementation of recommendations.

Victims’ families have also faced practical obstacles:

- fear of retaliation by police or military personnel;
- difficulty identifying individual officers hidden by uniforms or deployed in unfamiliar units;
- loss or hurried burial of bodies;
- inadequate autopsies and medical documentation;
- destruction of homes and personal records;
- poor witness-protection arrangements; and
- distrust of investigations conducted by the same institutions accused of abuse.

These problems make prompt evidence preservation essential. Ballistic testing, duty rosters, radio logs, ammunition records, deployment orders, hospital files, photographs, and witness statements can help establish whether particular units or officers were responsible.

## Calls for an impartial investigation

Human-rights organizations called on the federal and Plateau State authorities to conduct an investigation that was independent of the units implicated in the killings. An inquiry limited to internal police review would not provide sufficient public confidence, especially where MOPOL personnel themselves were accused.

A credible investigation would need to:

- examine killings by mobs as well as alleged unlawful killings by police and soldiers;
- determine whether a shoot-on-sight order was issued and identify its author;
- obtain operational orders, radio communications, deployment lists, and weapons records;
- conduct or review autopsies and ballistic examinations;
- identify commanding officers and the personnel deployed at specific locations;
- protect witnesses, survivors, and investigators from intimidation;
- publish findings and supporting reasoning;
- refer evidence of criminal conduct to independent prosecutors; and
- provide compensation and other remedies to victims and their families.

Impartiality also requires that investigators avoid treating religion as evidence of guilt. Muslim and Christian witnesses must receive equal access to the process, and findings should be based on corroborated evidence rather than communal narratives.

## Command responsibility and the duty to prosecute

Accountability should not stop with the officer who pulled the trigger. Investigators must examine the entire chain of command. Senior officials may bear responsibility if they gave an unlawful order or knowingly allowed a pattern of killings to continue. Commanders also have a duty to control personnel, investigate credible reports, and discipline or refer suspects for prosecution.

Conversely, criminal responsibility must be individualized. The fact that a unit was present in an area does not establish that every member committed a crime. Fair trials, reliable evidence, and the presumption of innocence remain essential even when public pressure for accountability is intense.

The goal of an impartial inquiry is therefore not collective punishment of MOPOL, the military, or any religious community. It is to establish who did what, under whose authority, and with what legal justification.

## Why accountability matters

The Jos riots were not an isolated tragedy. Further violence struck Plateau State in subsequent years, fueled by many of the same unresolved disputes and by a culture of impunity. When attackers and abusive security personnel are not held accountable, communities may conclude that protection depends on armed self-defense rather than the rule of law.

Failure to investigate the alleged MOPOL killings also damages trust in policing. Communities that fear arbitrary arrest or execution are less likely to share intelligence, report crimes, or cooperate with authorities during future emergencies. That, in turn, makes it harder to prevent violence.

A transparent investigation would serve several purposes: justice for victims, deterrence of future abuses, clarification of lawful rules of engagement, and restoration of public confidence. It could also distinguish legitimate security operations from unlawful acts, protecting officers who acted properly while exposing those who did not.

## Conclusion

The November 2008 Jos riots involved atrocities by communal mobs and an enormous failure of public security. But restoring order did not permit police or military personnel to execute detainees, unarmed civilians, or curfew violators. The allegations that MOPOL officers killed groups of young Muslim men—and that an official shoot-on-sight directive encouraged or enabled those killings—were too serious to be resolved through denials or internal reviews alone.

An independent, adequately resourced, and public investigation remains the appropriate response. It should establish the wording and origin of any lethal-force order, identify officers and commanders involved in unlawful killings, examine crimes committed against every community, and ensure fair prosecutions where the evidence supports them. Without that process, the victims’ families are denied justice and the conditions that allowed the violence to recur remain largely intact.
